final_answer:
Let
\[
t=\arctan s,\qquad 0<t<\frac{\pi}{2}.
\]
A direct computation gives
\[
\{\arctan s,s\}
=\frac{t'''}{t'}-\frac32\left(\frac{t''}{t'}\right)^2
=-\frac{2}{(1+s^2)^2}.
\]
So \(g\) and \(t=\arctan s\) have the same Schwarzian derivative.

Define
\[
F(t)=g(\tan t),\qquad 0<t<\frac{\pi}{2}.
\]
By the Schwarzian chain rule,
\[
\{F(t),t\}=0.
\]
Hence \(F\) is a fractional linear function:
\[
F(t)=\frac{at+b}{ct+d}.
\]
Since \(g(s)\to0\) as \(s\to0^+\), we have \(F(t)\to0\) as \(t\to0^+\), so \(b=0\). Thus
\[
F(t)=\frac{At}{1+Ct}.
\]
Also \(g(s)\to1\) as \(s\to\infty\), so with \(L=\frac{\pi}{2}\),
\[
F(L)=1,
\qquad\text{hence}\qquad
AL=1+CL.
\]

The condition \(g(s)+g(1/s)=1\) becomes
\[
F(t)+F(L-t)=1,
\]
because \(\arctan(1/s)=L-t\). Substituting \(F(t)=\frac{At}{1+Ct}\) gives
\[
\frac{At}{1+Ct}+\frac{A(L-t)}{1+C(L-t)}=1.
\]
Comparing coefficients in \(t(L-t)\) yields
\[
2AC=C^2.
\]
So either \(C=0\), or \(C=2A\). If \(C=2A\), then \(AL=1+2AL\), so \(A=-1/L<0\), contradicting \(g'(s)>0\). Therefore \(C=0\), and \(A=1/L=2/\pi\).

Thus
\[
g(s)=\frac{2}{\pi}\arctan s.
\]
Since \(g(s)=f(e^s)\), for \(x>1\), \(s=\log x\), so

\[
\boxed{f(x)=\frac{2}{\pi}\arctan(\log x)}.
\]
